candidates.title: Verifier-Calibrated Blocking for LLM-Generated NetOps Changes
candidates.research_question: Can combining claim-level calibration of LLM outputs with a deterministic network verifier reduce the rate of unsafe automated network changes compared to naïve LLM auto-application?
hypotheses: Integrating claim-level confidence calibration with deterministic verification will reduce the proportion of unsafe automated changes produced by an LLM by >50% relative to naïve auto-apply.

Using verifier-based blocking with a calibrated confidence threshold will limit the additional human-review workload (false-positive review requests) to a practically manageable level (<20% increase over baseline review volume).
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled, paired simulation experiment. Input set: 500 operator-intent tasks constructed from public configuration corpora (PreConfig-style public examples) and synthetically generated operational intents. Two agent conditions per task (paired): (A) Naïve LLM auto-apply: LLM translates intent to configuration and the change is applied (simulated) without verifier gating; (B) Calibrated+Verifier agent: LLM output is calibrated for claim-level confidence; deterministic network verifier (MEV-style verifier) checks the candidate change and either blocks, requests human review, or allows auto-apply according to preset thresholds. Calibration model and threshold chosen via 5-fold cross-validation on a held-out calibration split. Verifier returns pass/fail and explicit reachable-policy violations. Record per-task final state, verifier findings, and human-review flags. Randomize task order; fix random seeds; limit LLM output retries to one. Produce all raw artifacts (prompts, outputs, verifier traces).
candidates.expected_data: Per task: LLM-generated configuration, calibrated confidence score, verifier pass/fail flags, whether change would be applied/blocked/requested for human review, simulated post-change reachability/policy violations, time-to-decision. Aggregate: unsafe-apply count, safe-apply count, human-review request count, confusion matrices, latency distributions, and per-task logs for manual failure analysis.
candidates.primary_outcome: Relative reduction (%) in unsafe automated changes (unsafe-apply events) of Calibrated+Verifier vs Naïve LLM.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute paired proportions of unsafe-apply events per task; test difference with McNemar's test (paired binary outcomes) and report exact two-sided p-value and 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the relative reduction. Report precision/recall of human-review flags for catching unsafe changes, and false-positive rate (benign changes flagged). Secondary analyses: stratified safety reduction by intent complexity, calibration threshold sensitivity analysis, and latency trade-off plots. Report all raw counts and effect sizes.
risks: Verifier model mismatch (verifier abstraction may not capture all operational invariants) leading to false negatives
Calibration thresholds tuned on synthetic/held-out sets may not generalize to unseen intents
Simulator fidelity differences from production may mis-estimate real-world gains
Latency from verifier checks may be operationally unacceptable in low-latency workflows

candidates.title: Iterative Generate–Verify–Repair Loop for Automated Configuration Repair
candidates.research_question: Does an iterative generate–verify–repair loop improve the success rate of repairing network misconfigurations compared to single-shot LLM generation?
hypotheses: An iterative generate–verify–repair loop will achieve a higher absolute repair success rate than single-shot LLM generation on a corpus of misconfiguration tasks.
The median number of LLM repair iterations required for successful repair under the loop will be ≤3 for the majority (>75%) of solvable cases.
candidates.proposed_design: Dataset: 600 misconfiguration repair tasks synthesized from public configuration examples (PreConfig-like) and curated real-world-inspired failure cases (routing loops, ACL misorders, BGP export mistakes). Two methods evaluated per task (paired): (A) Single-shot: LLM given intent+fault produces one repair candidate; (B) Iterative GVR loop: LLM proposes repair → deterministic verifier checks → if verifier reports remaining violations the LLM receives verifier feedback and attempts repair again, up to max 5 iterations. Verifier used to accept final repair. Measure success if final configuration passes verifier checks and simulated functional tests. Fix random seeds and limit generation temperature; log all iterations, prompts, and verifier outputs.
candidates.expected_data: Per task: success/failure label, number of iterations (for GVR), sequence of generated repairs and verifier diagnostics, time per iteration. Aggregates: success rate per method, distribution of iterations to success, failure-mode taxonomy from verifier traces, repair correctness confusion matrices.
candidates.primary_outcome: Absolute difference in repair success rate (percentage points) between Iterative GVR and Single-shot methods.
candidates.analysis_outline: Paired proportion test (McNemar) for success/failure difference; Kaplan–Meier-like survival curve for cumulative probability of success by iteration count; bootstrap 95% CIs for median iterations; per-failure categorical analysis of verifier-produced failure types; sensitivity analysis by fault class. Report exact counts and effect sizes.
risks: Iteration may oscillate between syntactically different but semantically equivalent failed repairs (looping)
Verifier incompleteness may mark repaired configs as failing (false negatives), biasing results
Synthetic fault corpus may not capture production diversity limiting external validity
Compute budget could be exceeded if many tasks require maximal iterations

candidates.title: Compact Action-Aware Staging Benchmark to Evaluate End-to-End Safety of Agentic NetOps
candidates.research_question: Can a compact, action-aware benchmark that simulates staged rollouts, canaries, and rollback/audit processes reveal meaningful differences in end-to-end safety between verifier-augmented and LLM-only NetOps agents?
hypotheses: A compact action-aware benchmark that includes staged rollout and rollback simulation will detect statistically significant differences in end-to-end safety between verifier-augmented and LLM-only agents across realistic task sets.
Verifier-augmented agents will achieve higher end-to-end safe-deploy rates than LLM-only agents by a practically meaningful margin (>20% relative improvement) on the benchmark tasks.
candidates.proposed_design: Design a benchmark suite of 200 tasks representing common operational changes (ACL updates, route policy changes, QoS updates) with encoded deployment scenarios (full rollout, canary rollout windows, rollback triggers). Implement a sandboxed rollout simulator that applies changes to a simulated topology and enforces staged rollout semantics. Compare two agent implementations across the benchmark: (A) LLM-only agent that translates intent to change and executes staged rollout logic naively; (B) Verifier-augmented agent that uses a deterministic verifier at each rollout stage and blocks/rolls back on detected violations. Measure end-to-end safety metrics (safe-deploy rate, mean time to rollback, number of unintended disruptions) and auditability (completeness of change provenance). Use SSRN guidance and evaluation-gap literature to inform task selection and metrics.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task outcomes for each agent: safe-deploy boolean, time-to-rollback if triggered, number of affected flows/services, audit log completeness, and simulated user-impact metrics. Aggregates: safe-deploy rate, average rollback latency, distribution of affected services, and qualitative failure-mode annotations.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in safe-deploy rate (absolute and relative) between Verifier-augmented and LLM-only agents on the benchmark.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare safe-deploy rates with two-sample proportion tests and compute effect sizes (Cohen's h). Use permutation tests for robust p-values given finite benchmark size. Report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for mean time-to-rollback. Perform qualitative nearest-failure-mode clustering and provide representative artifact traces. Conduct ablation of canary sizes and rollback thresholds.
risks: Benchmark simulation may not capture full production interactions (external validity)
Small benchmark size risks overfitting agent heuristics
Defining canonical staged-rollout semantics across use cases is challenging and may bias results
Potentially high computational cost for multi-stage simulated rollouts

candidates.title: Robustness of LLM NetOps Agents to Adversarially Perturbed Operator Intents
candidates.research_question: How robust are LLM-based NetOps agents to adversarially perturbed operator intents that embed malicious or ambiguous constraints, and can verifier+calibration mitigate such adversarial success?
hypotheses: Adversarially perturbed operator intents will increase the rate of unsafe configuration proposals and successful unsafe-applies by LLM-only agents compared to benign intents.
Combining deterministic verification with claim-level calibration will significantly reduce adversarial attack success rate compared to an LLM-only pipeline.
candidates.proposed_design: Adversarial evaluation using 400 intent tasks derived from public corpora and a set of adversarial perturbation strategies drawn from recent adversarial-prompt literature. For each benign intent generate multiple adversarial variants (ambiguity injection, malicious constraint embedding, instruction-ordering attacks). Evaluate three agents per task: (A) LLM-only auto-apply, (B) LLM with claim-level calibration only, (C) LLM with calibration + deterministic verifier blocking. Measure attack success (unsafe change accepted), detection rate, false-positive human-review requests, and types of failure. Use logistic regression to model attack success as a function of agent type and perturbation strength.
candidates.expected_data: Per-case: benign/adversarial label, perturbation type and strength, agent outputs, calibrated scores, verifier diagnostics, accepted/blocked/applied outcome. Aggregates: attack success rates per agent and perturbation type, ROC/AUC for detection by calibration score, confusion matrices, and qualitative failure exemplars.
candidates.primary_outcome: Absolute reduction in adversarial attack success rate achieved by Calibration+Verifier vs LLM-only.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate attack success probabilities per agent and perturbation level; compare rates with two-sample proportion tests and compute odds ratios with 95% CIs. Fit logistic regression including interaction terms for agent×perturbation-strength and report p-values and model fit diagnostics. Present ROC curves for calibrated-score detection and report AUC. Conduct qualitative root-cause analysis on top failure clusters.
risks: Adversarial perturbation generation may not reflect realistic attacker capabilities (external validity)
Ethical considerations around publishing adversarial prompts; mitigated by simulated sandbox and harm-minimizing disclosure
Verifier or calibration may produce high false-positive rates under adversarial distribution, reducing operational utility
Adversarial examples may exploit verifier-model mismatches leading to unanticipated failures
